obtained.how: Internet Archive item sim_journal-of-wildlife-management_1949-10_13_4 (the October 1949 issue, Serials in Microfilm collection), openly downloadable, not a lending item; saved as Underhill_1949.issue.pdf and the article's PDF pages 45–61 indexed (Table 1 and Raney's table read on the page images)

bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the article's first page and running heads
bibliography.note: Underhill, A. H. 1949. Studies on the development, growth and maturity of the chain pickerel, Esox niger LeSueur. J. Wildl. Manage. 13(4): 377–391 (October 1949) — matches; drop '(via secondary sources)'. NOT the same item as FishBase's 'Underhill 1948': that is the Cornell Ph.D. thesis, 'Studies on the life history of the chain pickerel, Esox niger Lesueur', 177 p. (FishBase ref. 39106); the 1949 article says its material 'is incorporated in a thesis submitted to that university'

claims.claim: incubation 11 d at 10.0 °C, 5 d at 14.4 °C, 2.5 d at 17.2 °C (row sources include Underhill 1949)
claims.note: the 1949 article gives only 'six to twelve days', 'largely governed by the water temperature' (p. 379), with no temperature-specific points. FishBase's egg-development table credits 2.5 d at 17.2 °C to Underhill 1948 (the Cornell thesis, ref. 39106), 5 d at 14.4 °C to Jones, Martin & Hardy 1978 (ref. 4639) and 11 d at 10.0 °C to Miller 1962 (Trans. Am. Fish. Soc. 91(3): 323, ref. 39118), all under main ref. Jones et al. 1978. Cite those, not the 1949 article

Underhill gives one value, not this range: 18 newly hatched fry from 4 lots of artificially fertilized eggs averaged 6.1 mm TL (SD 0.19 mm) (p. 380). It lies inside 4.2–7.0 mm; the range itself must come from the Ontario database. The rewrite can cite '6.1 mm (Underhill 1949)'

claims.claim: fry hang on plants by a snout gland for ~1 week
claims.source_value: sac fry (yolk absorbed in 6–8 days) attach by 'the most anterior portion of the head', probably by a gummy secretion like the pike's (not studied); in aquaria most were attached at night and on the bottom by day; wild sac fry were never seen attached by day — they lay on their sides among roots, debris and silt — but many were attached to vegetation at night
claims.location: p. 379 (PDF p. 47); Plate 14A caption, p. 380 (PDF p. 48)
claims.quote: No detailed study was made of the mechanics of this attaching
claims.conditions: aquarium observations of six lots of fry and field observations of wild sac fry, central New York, 1930s
claims.note: the 'gland' is Underhill's inference, and the hanging is mostly a night behaviour; by day wild sac fry lie on the bottom. The model's larval habitat could follow that

claims.claim: first food at about 10 mm (Underhill 1949 via secondary sources)
claims.quote: fry measured as the yolk was absorbed and feeding commenced was 10.2
claims.conditions: mean TL 10.2 ± 0.32 mm of 14 fry (6 wild, 8 from artificially fertilized lots), measured when the yolk was absorbed and feeding began, 6–8 days after hatching
claims.note: now read in full; drop 'via secondary sources'

claims.claim: spawning at 6–11 °C on vegetation in shallow water; 2–3-mm adhesive eggs (row sources include Underhill 1949)
claims.note: Underhill gives no spawning temperature or egg size: in central New York pickerel 'usually spawns during the month of April', 'in swampy, marshy, or flooded areas' (pp. 379–380). Those values come from the row's other sources

claims.claim: the field's 25–38 mm at the end of June and 100–130 mm at the end of September (Underhill 1949 via Scott & Crossman)
claims.note: neither figure is in Underhill 1949. His Table 1 (p. 380, read on the page image), young-of-year mean TL: 27 mm (7 June 1939) and 19 mm (30 May 1940) at Willseyville Creek, 34 mm at Papish Pond (June 1939), 28.5 mm at Skaneateles Lake (9 June 1940); 53–60 mm in early–mid July (Willseyville 6 July 1940; Myosotis and Lincoln ponds 1937); 60–64 mm on 12 August 1940; 72–79 mm on 24–25 August 1940; 149 mm on 30 October 1939 (n = 3); 171 mm on 30 November 1939. Raney's 1939 pond series that he quotes (p. 378): 39 mm (30–50) on 30 June, 91 mm (81–119) on 22 September. Cite Scott & Crossman for 25–38 / 100–130 mm, or use Underhill's own series; either way the model's 4.4 cm by late September is far behind (Underhill: ~7.5 cm by late August)

notes: Lead resolved: FishBase's 'Underhill 1948' (the 2.5 d at 17.2 °C point) is the Cornell Ph.D. thesis, a different item; the 1949 article prints only 6–12 days. The article's usable values: hatch length 6.1 mm (n = 18); first feeding at 10.2 mm, 6–8 days after hatch; young-of-year growth series in Table 1 (above); maturity (pp. 386–388): at Willseyville Creek 3 of 15 one-year-old females and 12 of 24 one-year-old males mature, 12 of 14 and 15 of 18 two-year-olds; at Papish Pond most first spawn at age 4 (some males at 3); at Skaneateles 3 of 4 two-year-olds of each sex mature. Age-I lengths 17–19.5 cm TL in spring at Willseyville (Table 2); oldest fish 7 years, largest 1,389 g; weight–length exponents 3.04–3.54 (Table 7). Adult tag returns: 12 of 34 tagged Papish fish recaptured within a year (no population estimate).
